data.title: We Like The Quality Of Uniao Pet Participacoes' (BVMF:AUAU3) Earnings
data.description:
Uniao Pet Participacoes S.A.'s (BVMF:AUAU3) recent earnings report didn't offer any surprises, with the shares unchanged over the last week. We did some analysis to find out why and believe that investors might be missing some encouraging factors contained in the earnings.

AI is about to change healthcare. These 20 stocks are working on everything from early diagnostics to drug discovery. The best part - they are all under $10bn in marketcap - there is still time to get in early.

A Closer Look At Uniao Pet Participacoes' Earnings

Many investors haven't heard of the accrual ratio from cashflow, but it is actually a useful measure of how well a company's profit is backed up by free cash flow (FCF) during a given period. In plain english, this ratio subtracts FCF from net profit, and divides that number by the company's average operating assets over that period. This ratio tells us how much of a company's profit is not backed by free cashflow.

As a result, a negative accrual ratio is a positive for the company, and a positive accrual ratio is a negative. While having an accrual ratio above zero is of little concern, we do think it's worth noting when a company has a relatively high accrual ratio. That's because some academic studies have suggested that high accruals ratios tend to lead to lower profit or less profit growth.

Uniao Pet Participacoes has an accrual ratio of -0.33 for the year to September 2026. Therefore, its statutory earnings were very significantly less than its free cashflow. Indeed, in the last twelve months it reported free cash flow of R$799m, well over the R$220.2m it reported in profit. Uniao Pet Participacoes shareholders are no doubt pleased that free cash flow improved over the last twelve months.

That might leave you wondering what analysts are forecasting in terms of future profitability. Luckily, you can click here to see an interactive graph depicting future profitability, based on their estimates.

Our Take On Uniao Pet Participacoes' Profit Performance

Happily for shareholders, Uniao Pet Participacoes produced plenty of free cash flow to back up its statutory profit numbers. Because of this, we think Uniao Pet Participacoes' underlying earnings potential is as good as, or possibly even better, than the statutory profit makes it seem! Better yet, its EPS are growing strongly, which is nice to see. At the end of the day, it's essential to consider more than just the factors above, if you want to understand the company properly. Keep in mind, when it comes to analysing a stock it's worth noting the risks involved. With the stock now carrying a much larger market value than five years ago, the key issue is how that payout profile stacks up against the price you would be paying today.

Does Iberdrola Look Pricey on Dividends?

The Dividend Discount Model (DDM) values Iberdrola by projecting its future dividend stream and discounting that back to today. On this view, the key inputs are how fast the payout can grow and how much of earnings management is willing to share with investors. The model uses a dividend per share of €0.81, a return on equity of about 9.5% and a payout ratio near 20%, which together translate into a capped dividend growth rate of 3.06% a year.

That relatively modest growth cap matters because Iberdrola trades at €22.59, while the DDM projections put Iberdrola's estimated intrinsic value meaningfully below the current share price. A low payout today combined with expected growth above 7% in earnings implies more cash being retained inside the business, not necessarily flowing out as higher dividends. Because Iberdrola and peers are committing large amounts to US offshore wind projects, those capital needs help explain why a dividend-focused model could point below the market price. data.title: Learn Why The Bull Case For Frontline (FRO) Could Change Following Strong Quarterly Results
data.description:
• Frontline plc reported unaudited third quarter 2026 results with strong profit, declared a cash dividend, sold two VLCCs for US$270 million, paid a special dividend from net proceeds, and secured a new revolving credit facility with a lower interest margin.
  • The VLCC disposals and special dividend show Frontline using return on equity logic to recycle capital, while the cheaper revolving credit facility reshapes its funding mix and future flexibility.
  • We will now look at how Frontline's fresh dividend decision could influence the investment narrative that formed during earlier record quarters.

Scan how Frontline is recycling capital, then compare that playbook with a curated set of peers using the 35 high quality undervalued stocks as a starting point for further ideas.

Frontline Investment Narrative Recap

To own Frontline, you need to be comfortable with a tanker operator whose earnings are tightly tied to freight cycles and geopolitical trade flows. According to LunaRodas, an investor in the Simply Wall St Community, the key debate is how long the current market tightness can support very strong returns on equity. The latest profit and ordinary dividend keep that story intact, while the special dividend and vessel sales mostly fine tune capital deployment rather than changing the operating thesis.

The near term swing factor still sits in freight rates and fleet utilization rather than financial engineering. Forecasts point to revenue and earnings declining over the next three years, so the biggest risk is that current cash generation proves short lived while leverage and fleet commitments stay high. From that perspective, this quarter’s news looks important for liquidity and payouts but does not remove the core cyclicality that already sits in the Frontline narrative.

The freshest disclosure that really matters here is the sale of two VLCCs for US$270 million and the decision to send the net cash to investors via a special dividend. That move ties directly to what LunaRodas argued about asset sales becoming an explicit expression of capital allocation discipline, with management using a return on equity lens to judge whether to hold or sell ships.

The new revolving credit facility with a lower interest margin also feeds into the same catalyst set. Cheaper committed debt can give Frontline more room to handle rate volatility while keeping fleet optionality, although it does not remove the risks linked to high leverage and an unstable dividend track record. For readers, the combination of asset recycling, ordinary payouts and special dividends sets up a clear tension between current cash returns and forecast earnings declines.

TheGapReport assigns a fair value of US$34.07 to Frontline, with LunaRodas framing that figure as the narrative’s own anchor based on how current tanker conditions, idle VLCC capacity and management’s capital allocation choices intersect to sustain what is described as an ocean of profits.

data.title: We Think That There Are More Issues For CSN Mineração (BVMF:CMIN3) Than Just Sluggish Earnings
data.description:
Last week's earnings announcement from CSN Mineração S.A. (BVMF:CMIN3) was disappointing to investors, with a sluggish profit figure. We did some analysis, and found that there are some reasons to be cautious about the headline numbers.

We've found 21 US stocks that are forecast to pay a dividend yield of over 6% next year. See the full list for free.

A Closer Look At CSN Mineração's Earnings

As finance nerds would already know, the accrual ratio from cashflow is a key measure for assessing how well a company's free cash flow (FCF) matches its profit. The accrual ratio subtracts the FCF from the profit for a given period, and divides the result by the average operating assets of the company over that time. You could think of the accrual ratio from cashflow as the 'non-FCF profit ratio'.

That means a negative accrual ratio is a good thing, because it shows that the company is bringing in more free cash flow than its profit would suggest. While it's not a problem to have a positive accrual ratio, indicating a certain level of non-cash profits, a high accrual ratio is arguably a bad thing, because it indicates paper profits are not matched by cash flow. To quote a 2014 paper by Lewellen and Resutek, "firms with higher accruals tend to be less profitable in the future".

Over the twelve months to September 2026, CSN Mineração recorded an accrual ratio of 0.51. Statistically speaking, that's a real negative for future earnings. And indeed, during the period the company didn't produce any free cash flow whatsoever. Over the last year it actually had negative free cash flow of R$2.5b, in contrast to the aforementioned profit of R$1.28b. We saw that FCF was R$3.1b a year ago though, so CSN Mineração has at least been able to generate positive FCF in the past. The good news for shareholders is that CSN Mineração's accrual ratio was much better last year, so this year's poor reading might simply be a case of a short term mismatch between profit and FCF. Shareholders should look for improved cashflow relative to profit in the current year, if that is indeed the case.

That might leave you wondering what analysts are forecasting in terms of future profitability. Luckily, you can click here to see an interactive graph depicting future profitability, based on their estimates.

Our Take On CSN Mineração's Profit Performance

As we discussed above, we think CSN Mineração's earnings were not supported by free cash flow, which might concern some investors. For this reason, we think that CSN Mineração's statutory profits may be a bad guide to its underlying earnings power, and might give investors an overly positive impression of the company. But at least holders can take some solace from the 5.7% EPS growth in the last year. The Impact Of Unusual Items On Profit

For anyone who wants to understand Equatorial's profit beyond the statutory numbers, it's important to note that during the last twelve months statutory profit was reduced by R$3.1b due to unusual items. While deductions due to unusual items are disappointing in the first instance, there is a silver lining. We looked at thousands of listed companies and found that unusual items are very often one-off in nature. And, after all, that's exactly what the accounting terminology implies. If Equatorial doesn't see those unusual expenses repeat, then all else being equal we'd expect its profit to increase over the coming year.
